audience: Engineers with basic programming knowledge learning databases. Explain concepts directly and connect their mechanisms, consequences and design choices. Examples are optional when they clarify a concept; assessment does not require a recurring application, brand names or an example on every card.
prerequisites: A program runs instructions, holds data in memory and can call other code; separate processes do not automatically share their memory.
A network can carry messages between computers, and messages can be delayed or fail to arrive.
An HTTP request has a method, URL, headers and optional body; its response has a status, headers and optional body.
A client requests work from a server; a database stores data that an application can read and change.

objectives.description: Explain managed persistent data, query/update operations and how data access requirements affect system design.
Choose a database from data relationships, access patterns, correctness rules and operational constraints.
Compare relational tables, documents and key-value records by representation and access patterns.
Explain wide-column partition access, graph traversal and vector similarity as distinct query-oriented capabilities.
Explain that relational databases can also support geospatial and vector operations and evaluate actual features before adding a separate data store.
Connect indexing, data duplication and distribution choices to their write, storage and coordination costs.
Bound CAP to replicated data during network partitions and distinguish its consistency and availability meanings from everyday labels.
Build a requirement-to-capability-to-cost explanation and identify what evidence could change the decision.

questions.question: Define a database and explain its responsibilities for storing, finding and updating data beyond a program's temporary memory. Why do query patterns and correctness requirements influence the surrounding application, and why is a database not an automatic guarantee against all data loss? Before choosing a database, what must you learn about data shape and relationships, common queries and updates, correctness rules, scale and operations? Explain why a product name or SQL-versus-NoSQL label is insufficient.
criteria: A database manages stored data and operations for retrieving and changing it; persistent data can outlive an application process.
How data is represented and accessed affects application queries, updates and correctness rules.
Persistence relies on configured storage and recovery behavior; failures and accidental changes still require operational protection.
Identify entities or records, relationships, lookup/filter/aggregation patterns and how updates occur.
Identify rules that must hold across changes, expected data and traffic growth, latency needs and the ability to operate and recover the system.
A category or brand alone does not establish support for the actual access patterns, guarantees and deployment constraints.

questions.question: Describe relational tables, document records and key-value records. Explain relationships and joins at a basic level, when reading a grouped document or directly looking up a key is useful, and why model choice changes query/update work without giving a universal ranking. Explain wide-column partition access, graph traversal and vector similarity. Define a data partition key, graph nodes and edges, and an embedding/vector at the level needed to understand those queries. Connect each structure to the question it serves, and explain why vector similarity does not prove factual correctness or exact equality.
criteria: Relational data uses rows and columns; relationships connect records, and joins combine matching related records for a query.
Documents group fields and nested data as a record, useful for reading related data together; duplicated data can require coordinated updates.
Key-value access retrieves a value by key efficiently for that access pattern, while other queries depend on additional capabilities or structures. Each model has workload-dependent costs.

Wide-column layouts organize rows by a partition key that groups data for targeted access; query requirements must fit that organization. A data partition is a grouping of records, distinct from a network communication failure.
Graphs represent entities as nodes and relationships as edges, supporting traversal along connections.

An embedding represents an item as a numeric vector; similarity search finds nearby vectors under a chosen measure, which can support semantic retrieval but does not prove exact equality or factual correctness.

questions.question: Explain how a relational database can also support geospatial queries and vector similarity. Define what each capability queries, and explain how to decide whether an existing database's capability is sufficient and what costs a separate specialized store adds. Does support for a feature prove equal performance or guarantees? Define an index and explain how it can improve reads while costing storage and write work. Explain why duplicating data can simplify reads but complicate updates, and why distributing data may increase capacity or resilience while adding network and coordination costs. Does any one model remove these trade-offs?
criteria: Database categories describe common strengths rather than exclusive capabilities; relational storage can also provide location or spatial relationship queries and vector similarity through built-in features or extensions.
Assess actual query support, guarantees and representative workload performance rather than infer equivalence from a feature name; no particular vendor or extension name is required.
A separate store adds data movement or synchronization, operations and possible disagreement between copies, so it needs a demonstrated benefit.
An index is an extra access structure that helps locate relevant data without examining every record for suitable queries, at the cost of space and maintenance on writes.
Duplication can avoid repeated assembly on reads but requires keeping multiple representations consistent when data changes.
Distribution introduces remote communication, partial failures and coordination as well as potential capacity or resilience benefits; no model eliminates all trade-offs.

questions.question: Define replication and a network partition at a basic level. When communication splits copies, what do CAP consistency and availability mean and why can they not both be guaranteed for all affected operations? Explain why this is not a general rule to choose any two letters and why it does not classify every database deployment identically. Give a compact method for defending a database choice: connect required queries and data rules to a model or capability, state an accepted cost, address relevant failure behavior and identify measurements or changed requirements that could force reconsideration. Must the answer name a particular vendor or use multiple databases?
criteria: Replication keeps copies of data; a partition prevents required communication between some nodes while nodes can remain running.

CAP consistency is behavior as one current copy with completed writes reflected in later reads; availability requires requests to non-failing nodes to complete with the operation's response. An isolated node cannot both learn an unreachable completed write and answer every relevant request.

The conflict applies during partitions to affected operations; refusing or delaying them can preserve consistency, while continuing can sacrifice it. Guarantees depend on configuration and operation rather than a universal product label.
The reasoning starts from data, queries and correctness needs and ties these to capabilities rather than popularity.
It states a concrete write, storage, coordination or operating cost and relevant recovery or partition behavior.
Representative workload measurements and changed access/scale requirements can change the decision; naming a brand or adding multiple databases is not necessary.
criticalMisconceptions: CAP means always choose any two of C, A and P.
